tagline.text: Mother of the Jondrette family in the Gorbeau house, who loves her daughters and not her son.
The Jondrettes' huge, red-haired wife, crouched by a dying fire in their garret.
Her husband's partner in the plan he hatches against their benefactor.

description.text: The mother of the destitute Jondrette household in the Gorbeau hovel: a family of four in one attic room. When her son Little Gavroche comes home every few months he finds a cold hearth; his mother loves his sisters, not him.

Seen by Marius through the hole in the wall, she is a giant of a woman beside her small husband, forty or a hundred years old, squatting barefoot by the fire in chemise and petticoat, with greying reddish-blond hair and huge shining hands, a volume of a sentimental romance open on the floor. She calls her raging husband her 'little friend' and tells him he is too good to write to all those people.
When the gentleman from Saint-Jacques is announced she obeys her husband's orders to go to bed and play the invalid, and comforts the younger girl after she cuts her hand on the broken pane.
During M. Leblanc's visit her husband twice whispers to her to take a good look at the man.

Alone with her, Jondrette says he recognises the visitor from eight years ago and whispers something about the young lady that throws her into a rage. She is with him in the plan: the man will come back at six, and if he does not give in, 'we'll fix him'.

On the night of the trap she is dressed absurdly in a plumed black bonnet and a vast tartan shawl, takes Marius's two chairs from his room without seeing him, and goes down with a lantern to let the visitor in and send his cab away.
She places herself between M. Leblanc and the door, and when he says Madame Fabantou seems better she calls her husband 'Monsieur Jondrette' by mistake.

moments.text: Hears her husband's plan and joins it.
Lights M. Leblanc up the stairs on the night of the trap.

name: The man in the yellow coat

tagline.text: A silent stranger who lifts Cosette's bucket in the dark forest.
A poor, very clean white-haired traveller who avoids the king's carriage and the police on Christmas Day 1823.
The shabby guest at the Thénardiers' inn who gives Cosette a doll.
The stranger who pays fifteen hundred francs and walks away with Cosette.

description.text: As Cosette staggers back from the spring in the dark with her bucket, a huge hand silently lifts the weight from her. A man is walking beside her, and she is not afraid.

That Christmas afternoon he had been seen on the deserted Boulevard de l'Hôpital in Paris, looking for a lodging: a man in a threadbare ochre-yellow coat and an old round hat, poor but scrupulously clean, white-haired but strong in his stride. He hid from Louis XVIII's passing carriage, shook off the police agent sent after him, took the Lagny coach and got down at Chelles after dark. In the Montfermeil forest he went straight to a clearing with a heap of stones and marked trees, and checked that the ground there had not been disturbed.

Walking back with Cosette, he asks her questions: she is eight, works for Madame Thénardier, has no mother that she knows of. At her name he seems to receive a shock. He says he will lodge at the inn.

The Thénardiers take him for a beggar and charge him double. He watches Cosette all evening, spares her the whip by 'finding' a coin on the floor, buys the stocking she is knitting so that she may play, and when she is caught with the other girls' doll he goes out and comes back with the great doll from the stall. In the night he finds her asleep under the stairs and puts a gold louis in her wooden shoe.

Next morning he pays a bill of twenty-three francs without a word, asks whether they would like to be rid of the child, and lays fifteen hundred francs on the table. He dresses Cosette in mourning clothes from his bundle and walks out of Montfermeil with her.

When Thénardier catches up in the forest to demand more, the stranger produces a paper signed by Fantine ordering that the child be handed to the bearer, shows that Thénardier has already been overpaid, and walks off into the woods with Cosette and his cudgel.

moments.text: Lifts Cosette's bucket at the spring.
Gives Cosette the doll and a gold louis in her shoe.
Pays fifteen hundred francs and takes Cosette away.
Shows Thénardier a note signed by Fantine.

tagline.text: The Thénardiers' unloved little son, crying unheard in the inn on Christmas Eve 1823.

description.text: A boy of a little over three, born to the Thénardiers one winter, 'the result of the cold', his mother says. She nursed him but does not love him. When his crying annoys Thénardier, his wife answers, 'Bah! he bothers me,' and the child goes on shrieking in the dark.
In the night the stranger sees him asleep in an uncurtained wicker cradle behind Éponine and Azelma's beds, the little boy who had cried all evening.

tagline.text: The Emperor of the French, whose chance word made an obscure curé Bishop of Digne.
The fallen Emperor: the royalist Bishop snubbed him, but Digne still adores him.
The Emperor at Waterloo, 18 June 1815, at the centre of Hugo's long digression on the battle.
The great captain whose last battle Hugo puts down to rain, a hollow road and God.
Caged on Saint Helena, and looming larger in his fall than on his throne.

description.text: Napoleon Bonaparte, Emperor of the French from 1804 to 1815. Waiting in Cardinal Fesch's anteroom in 1804, the curé Myriel caught his eye and told him that he was looking at a good man and the good man at a great one. Soon afterwards Myriel was astonished to find himself Bishop of Digne.

He made the Bishop a baron and summoned him to the synod of 1811. The Bishop, a royalist, applauded his fall, refused to see him on his return from Elba and ordered no prayers for him during the Hundred Days; the narrator counts this coldness the Bishop's one fault. The old soldiers of the Empire, like the town-hall porter, still swear by him.
In 1817 he is at Saint Helena, turning his old coats, while the Restoration paints fleurs-de-lys over Paris.

Hugo's Waterloo digression begins with him. Ill but in high spirits, sure of ninety chances in a hundred, he plans a battle Hugo admires; the night's rain delays his artillery until half-past eleven and gives the Prussians time to come. Hugo denies that his genius had failed.

Seeing Wellington's line pull back behind the crest, he takes it for a retreat, sends word of victory to Paris, and, after a shake of the head from his guide Lacoste, orders the cuirassiers to take the plateau. He never saw the hollow road of Ohain.
At nightfall, with his army dissolving, Bertrand and Bernard catch him by the coat in a meadow near Genappe, haggard, leading his horse, turning back alone toward Waterloo.

Hugo sees the Restoration as built on his defeat: the Bourbons back in the Tuileries, the Holy Alliance in charge of Europe, and Bonaparte on Saint Helena, larger in exile than ever, while the kings reign uneasily.
In 1832 he is still the talk of barbers' shops: an old soldier being shaved remembers how badly he rode and how he never fell.

moments.text: Makes the curé Myriel Bishop of Digne.
Orders the cuirassiers' charge onto the plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean.
Turns back alone toward the lost battlefield.

tagline.text: The British commander at Waterloo, holding the high ground of Mont-Saint-Jean.
The Iron Duke under his elm, murmuring 'Blücher, or night!'
A second-rate captain, Hugo says, who won a first-rate battle.

description.text: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington, commander of the Anglo-allied army at Waterloo. In Hugo's capital-A plan of the field he holds the apex, the plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean, while Napoleon holds the low ground.
By four o'clock his army is in grave trouble, but he stays coldly heroic under his elm and draws his line back behind the crest. Napoleon takes the movement for a retreat.
His squares hold for two hours against the cuirassiers, though seven of thirteen are destroyed and his staff decimated. At five he murmurs, 'Blücher, or night!'

Weighing the commanders, Hugo sets his calculation against Napoleon's genius, calls Waterloo a first-rate battle won by a second-rate captain, and gives the glory to the English soldier rather than to the Duke.
After the battle he has ordered marauders shot, but the prowlers strip the dead under the moon all the same.

tagline.text: The Prussian field marshal whose arrival decides Waterloo.
The Prussian commander who orders the French fugitives cut down without quarter.

description.text: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, commander of the Prussian army in 1815. Hugo argues that the rain delaying Napoleon's attack gave him time to reach the field.

At five o'clock, seeing Wellington's peril, he orders Bülow to attack: 'We must give air to the English army.' In the rout he orders extermination, and the Prussian cavalry hunts the fleeing French to the frontier.

tagline.text: Blücher's lieutenant, whose Prussian corps comes out of the forest at Plancenoit.

description.text: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow, commanding a Prussian corps. Delayed all day by mud and a burning bridge at Wavre, he is guided by a little shepherd along the one route that could bring guns out of the forest below Plancenoit. By another road, Hugo says, he would not have arrived, and Napoleon would have won.

tagline.text: The French marshal sent after the Prussians, who never comes to Waterloo.

description.text: Emmanuel de Grouchy, Marshal of France, detached with part of the army to pursue the Prussians. His delay is one of the morning's setbacks Napoleon shrugs off.
At noon Napoleon saw a 'cloud' on the horizon and was told it was Grouchy. It was the Prussians.

tagline.text: Marshal Ney, commanding the French attack at Waterloo.
Ney, bleeding and magnificent, seeking death on the field and failing to find it.

description.text: Michel Ney, Marshal of France and one of Napoleon's commanders on the day. At the opening of the battle he pushes the French right against the English left at Papelotte.
He draws his sword and leads the three thousand five hundred cuirassiers up the slope toward the English squares, where the hollow road of Ohain swallows the first ranks.

As the Guard is cut down he offers himself to every blow, his fifth horse killed under him, bleeding and magnificent, crying 'Come and see how a Marshal of France dies on the field of battle!' He does not die.
In the rout he leaps on a borrowed horse, without hat, cravat or sword, and tries to stop the flight across the Brussels road, and is swept away.

tagline.text: An obscure officer of the Guard who answers the call to surrender with one obscene word.
To Hugo, the true victor of Waterloo.

description.text: Pierre Cambronne, commanding the last square of the Imperial Guard at nine in the evening at the foot of Mont-Saint-Jean. When an English general calls on the brave Frenchmen to surrender, he answers with a single soldier's obscenity.
Hugo defends repeating the word and calls it perhaps the finest thing a Frenchman ever said: scorn answering catastrophe. The English guns fire, and when the smoke clears the square is gone.

tagline.text: The Bourbon king, waiting out Waterloo at Ghent.
The restored king, back in the Tuileries with the white flag and a charter.
The fat, gouty king whose gilded carriage gallops along the Paris boulevards.

description.text: Louis XVIII, brother of the guillotined Louis XVI, restored to the throne in 1814 and driven out by Napoleon's return from Elba. The panic of the battle's afternoon reaches him at Ghent.
After Waterloo he returns to the Tuileries; Hugo sketches the Restoration as divine right varnished with a charter, a counter-revolution forced to be liberal in spite of itself.
In 1823 he drives nearly every day to Choisy-le-Roi, a fat, crafty-eyed king who cannot walk and so loves to gallop. The people of the quarter call him 'the government'.

tagline.text: The Duc d'Orléans, made King of the French by the men of 1830 to say 'Halt' to the revolution.
The bourgeois king: in Hugo's portrait a good man and a good prince, if too much a paternal king.

description.text: Louis Philippe d'Orléans, of the younger branch of the Bourbons. When the July Revolution of 1830 overthrew Charles X, the bourgeoisie and the 'statesmen' needed a man to stop it halfway, a revolution and a stability at once. The 221 deputies made him king and Lafayette crowned him at the Hôtel de Ville, calling it 'the best of republics'.

Hugo's long portrait: careful, sober, patient and brave, a king in broad daylight who went out with his umbrella under his arm. Exile had recommended him to the throne: he had sold a horse for bread in Switzerland and taught mathematics at Reichenau. Hugo charges royalty and the reign with the repression of the street, but testifies for the man, who sat up at night revising death sentences and fought the guillotine case by case.
On 5 June 1832, with a third of Paris in the insurgents' hands, he remains serene.

tagline.text: The old hero of two revolutions, who bids Lamarque farewell at the Austerlitz bridge.

description.text: The Marquis de Lafayette, veteran of the American War of Independence and of 1789, who had crowned Louis Philippe at the Hôtel de Ville in 1830. At Lamarque's funeral on 5 June 1832 he speaks the farewell at the Austerlitz bridge. When a horseman with a red flag appears he turns away; the crowd shouts 'Lafayette to the Town-hall!' and drags his carriage along the Quai Morland.
Among the rumours that night: Lafayette, ill as he is, has said he will follow wherever there is room for a chair.

tagline.text: The general whose funeral Marius's friends are going to on 5 June 1832.
Soldier of the Empire and opposition deputy, whose funeral sets Paris alight.

description.text: Jean-Maximilien Lamarque, a general of the Empire and a liberal deputy. On the morning of 5 June 1832 Courfeyrac, Enjolras, Feuilly and Combeferre are setting out for his funeral, and ask Marius to come.

He had the bravery of the battlefield under the Empire and of the tribune under the Restoration, hated Wellington, kept the sadness of Waterloo for seventeen years, and died clasping a sword given him by the officers of the Hundred Days. The people dreaded his death as a loss, the government as an occasion. His funeral procession, crossing an armed and restless Paris, is the spark of the June rising.

tagline.text: The great Paris banker, to whom a letter is posted in haste from Montreuil-sur-Mer.
The banker from whom more than half a million francs was withdrawn before the mayor's arrest.

description.text: Jacques Laffitte, the most famous banker in Paris, governor of the Bank of France and a liberal deputy. Back from Arras before dawn, Jean Valjean posts a letter to him before going to Fantine.
The royalist paper reports that before his arrest the former mayor withdrew more than half a million francs, honestly earned, from M. Laffitte, and that no one knows where he has hidden it.

tagline.text: The old novelist and educator who spent six months as a lady resident at the Petit-Picpus.

description.text: Félicité de Genlis, novelist, educator of the Orléans princes and a famous literary figure of the old regime. Around 1820 she asked to enter the convent as a lady resident on the Duc d'Orléans's recommendation; the vocal mothers fluttered because she wrote romances, but she said she detested them. Very old, still playing the harp, superstitious and a Latinist, she left after six or eight months complaining that the garden had no shade, and left pasted in a cupboard five lines of Latin verse meant to frighten away robbers.
The convent's bell code gave her her own peal: four-four, heard very often.

tagline.text: A young priest of high rank, once a musketeer, whose sermon draws a cry from the mad Madame Albertine.

description.text: Louis-François-Auguste de Rohan-Chabot: officer of the Red Musketeers in 1815 as Prince de Léon, then a priest, peer of France and vicar-general of the Archbishop of Paris, dying in 1830 as cardinal and Archbishop of Besançon. When he first preaches at the Petit-Picpus, Madame Albertine half rises and cries 'Ah! Auguste!', and his name really is Auguste. The schoolgirls, who cannot see him through the curtain, know his sweet, shrill voice and dream of his well-dressed hair and elegant cassock.

tagline.text: The Archbishop of Paris, who grants a bold schoolgirl three days' leave.

description.text: Hyacinthe-Louis de Quélen, Archbishop of Paris from 1821. On one of his visits to the Petit-Picpus, when Mademoiselle Bouchard steps out of the ranks to ask for a day's leave, he smiles and grants her three, and the prioress can do nothing.

tagline.text: An old count of Madame de T.'s salon, respected as 'the Lamothe of the affair of the necklace'.

description.text: Husband of the Comtesse de la Motte, who swindled a cardinal over a diamond necklace in the scandal that disgraced Marie Antoinette's court in 1785. In 1815 he is seventy-five, silent and sententious, cold and angular, with polished manners and long legs in burnt-sienna trousers. He is the other oracle of Madame de T.'s royalist salon beside M. Gillenormand, held in consideration for his 'celebrity' and, strangely, for his name of Valois.

tagline.text: The man who first explored the sewers of Paris, 'the most intrepid man in the Empire'.
The forgotten man behind the revolution in the Paris sewer.

description.text: Pierre-Emmanuel Bruneseau, an official of the Paris sanitation service under the Empire. In 1805 the Minister of the Interior told Napoleon he had met the most intrepid man in the Empire: a man who wanted to visit the sewers, which even the police feared to enter.

From 1805 to 1812 he led a seven-year campaign underground against pestilence and suffocation. Some labourers refused, men fainted and vanished into holes; he read dated stones marking the work of earlier centuries and found an orang-utan's skeleton and, hanging from a grating's hinge, a rag of fine batiste that was a scrap of Marat's shroud.
The clean, straight modern sewer, Hugo says, is his work, though everyone has forgotten him.

tagline.text: A senator of the Empire near Digne who complains of the Bishop's carriage allowance.
The self-made 'philosopher' senator who preaches materialism to the Bishop over dessert.

description.text: A senator of the Empire, once of the Council of the Five Hundred, with a fine senatorial seat near Digne. When the Bishop claims his allowance for carriage and journeys, he writes an angry note to the minister of public worship: these priests are all greedy, and he is for Caesar alone.

A clever old attorney who made his way without letting conscience or sworn faith get in the road, kind to his relations, and educated just enough to think himself a disciple of Epicurus. Slightly drunk at the prefect's table, he expounds to the Bishop a materialism that frees a man from all scruple. The Bishop applauds him with irony: a fine philosophy for great lords, which lets them devour everything with an easy conscience, while belief in God is left to the people like the goose stuffed with chestnuts that is the poor man's truffled turkey.

tagline.text: A countess related to the Bishop who loves to list her sons' 'expectations'.

description.text: The Comtesse de Lô, a distant relative of the Bishop, often recites in front of him the inheritances awaiting her three sons from old relations near death. Once he answers with a saying from St Augustine: 'Place your hopes in the man from whom you do not inherit.'

tagline.text: A rich retired cloth merchant of Digne who gives one sou a week after a sermon on hell.

description.text: A wealthy retired merchant and part-time usurer who made two millions in coarse cloth and never gave alms in his life. After a young vicar's Lenten sermon on hellfire he gives a sou every Sunday to the six old beggar-women at the cathedral door. The Bishop, seeing it, remarks: 'There is M. Géborand purchasing paradise for a sou.'

tagline.text: A rich, miserly old marquis of Digne who refuses the Bishop's collection for the poor.

description.text: A wealthy, avaricious old man, at once ultra-royalist and ultra-Voltairian. When the Bishop begs from him in a Digne drawing-room he answers that he has poor people of his own. 'Give them to me,' says the Bishop.

tagline.text: A former fairground showman condemned to death at Digne, whom the Bishop attends to the scaffold.

description.text: A wretched man, once a mountebank at fairs and a public letter-writer, condemned for murder. The prison chaplain is ill and the curé refuses to attend 'that mountebank', so the Bishop goes himself, spends the whole day and night with him and turns his despair to light. Next morning he walks beside him through the crowd to the guillotine in his purple camail.

tagline.text: An old guardsman of Austerlitz who lost his post for insulting Louis XVIII; the Bishop made him beadle.

description.text: Porter of the Digne town-hall, placed there by the Emperor: a non-commissioned officer of the Old Guard, decorated at Austerlitz, a Bonapartist to the bone. He picked the Emperor's head out of his cross rather than wear the Bourbon lilies, and scoffed so loudly at 'the gouty old creature in English gaiters' that he lost his place, with a wife and children to feed. The royalist Bishop reproved him gently and made him beadle of the cathedral.

tagline.text: The 'good woman' who points the rejected stranger to the Bishop's door.

description.text: Coming out of the church at night, an old woman finds a man stretched on a stone bench in the cold. He tells her he has knocked at every door in Digne and been driven away; she gives him the four sous in her purse, then points across the street to the small low house beside the bishop's palace and asks whether he has knocked there.

moments.text: Sends the stranger to knock at the Bishop's door.

tagline.text: Landlord of the Cross of Colbas, the best inn in Digne, who turns the stranger out.

description.text: A man of standing in Digne through his kinsman who keeps the Three Dauphins inn at Grenoble, where Bertrand was said to have plotted the Emperor's return. When the dusty traveller asks for supper, he sends a scribbled note to the town-hall, reads the answer, and tells the man there is no room; when he insists, the host names him, Jean Valjean, and shows him the paper. He is polite to everyone, he says: go away.
Madame Magloire's gossip has it that a dangerous vagabond tried Labarre's inn and was refused.

tagline.text: A poor woman of Digne who calls at the Bishop's door with her baby during supper.

description.text: In Mademoiselle Baptistine's letter, she knocks during the meal with her little one in her arms. The Bishop kisses the child and borrows fifteen sous from his sister to give her.

tagline.text: Jean Valjean's widowed elder sister, left with seven children when he was sent to the galleys.

description.text: Older than her brother, she brought him up after their parents died; widowed with seven children, she was in turn kept by his work as a tree-pruner at Faverolles, and would slip the best of his soup into her children's bowls while he pretended not to see. It was for her starving children that he broke the baker's window. After he was taken, the family scattered. In his fourth year at Toulon he heard of her once: in Paris, near Saint-Sulpice, with only her youngest boy, folding sheets in a printing office from six in the morning while the child waited an hour in the dark courtyard for the school to open. He never heard of her again.

tagline.text: The baker of Faverolles whose window Jean Valjean broke for a loaf of bread.

description.text: Baker on the Church Square at Faverolles. One Sunday evening in a hard winter he heard his shop grating struck, saw an arm come through the broken glass and take a loaf, and ran the thief down: it was Jean Valjean, his arm still bleeding.

moments.text: Catches Jean Valjean stealing a loaf.
